messages:
danielle choi: hey team  first week! opened a PR from my fork to trigger CI but GitHub Actions didn't run and Buildkite passed when rachel triggered it manually. what's the usual flow for forks?

rachel kim: welcome danielle! in our org GH Actions are configured to not run workflows that need org secrets on PRs from forks (for security). Buildkite handles forks if you push a branch to the org remote, otherwise we manually trigger. can you share the PR link?

danielle choi: PR: https://github.com/redwood/my-service/pull/99
GH UI shows: "Some checks were not run" and the Actions tab says: "Workflows have not been triggered because this is a fork and the workflow uses secrets or write permissions."

piotr nowak: yep that's expected. two common patterns for new hires: (1) push your branch to the upstream org (create a branch on redwood/my-service) and open a PR from that branch, or (2) ask infra to temporarily enable `workflow_run` or a manual `workflow_dispatch` that doesn't require secrets. we avoid granting secrets to forked workflows by policy.

devops-bot: Tip: For security, GitHub blocks workflows from public forks from accessing secrets. If you need CI with secrets (e.g., publishing or accessing internal registries), push a branch to the org or request a manual Buildkite run.

danielle choi: i forked and pushed because i didn't have push perms on the org. rachel you said you triggered Buildkite manually earlier  could you walk me through that?

rachel kim: sure. I have a helper script infra uses: `scripts/ci/trigger-buildkite.sh <org-branch>` that triggers the onboarding pipeline against your fork branch. but the preferred is to push the branch to the org remote so all checks run automatically. i'll give you push access to `my-service` (ci-developers) in a moment.

security-bot: Note: Before granting push access, ensure your GitHub SSO is approved. If SSO is not approved, the org will block write permissions even if you're in the group.

piotr nowak: also watch out for workflows that need `GITHUB_TOKEN` write access; some of our merge automations require that. those won't be allowed on forked PRs. If you need those to run, we either do a manual run or create a short-lived branch on the org for the PR.

danielle choi: thanks! rachel i accepted the invite to ci-developers. pushed a branch `onboard/danielle/ci-fix` to the org. new PR: https://github.com/redwood/my-service/pull/100

(30s later)

danielle choi: looks like Actions kicked off and Buildkite also triggered automatically. one of the jobs failed with: `Error: could not read GITHUB_TOKEN permissions to write labels` during the merge-check step.

rachel kim: that step uses `GITHUB_TOKEN` with repo write perms to apply labels and update PR metadata. by default GH sets a restrictive token for workflows triggered by pull_request, you need `permissions: contents: write, checks: write` in the workflow to allow that. i'll patch the workflow to explicitly set needed permissions.

piotr nowak: quick example we use in `ci/.github/workflows/merge-check.yml`:
```
permissions:
  checks: write
  contents: write
  issues: write
```
Make sure the workflow isn't `pull_request_target` unless you intentionally want to run with elevated privileges (risky).

danielle choi: ack. thanks for the pointer. anything I should add to my personal onboarding notes?

rachel kim: add: (1) forks won't run workflows that use org secrets; push to org branch when possible, (2) accept org GitHub app + SSO, (3) if Actions 404s or shows "not run" check webhook delivery and app install, (4) if a job fails due to GITHUB_TOKEN perms, open a PR to update the workflow permissions or ask a maintainer to patch it.

security-bot: Reminder: When updating workflow permissions, follow the least-privilege principle. Review any request to change `permissions:` and run a quick security review if it expands write access.

danielle choi: thanks everyone 60a this cleared up a lot. rachel appreciate the push access and the walkthrough.

rachel kim: welcome aboard! i'll add a short note to the CI onboarding doc with the fork vs org-branch flow and the GITHUB_TOKEN perms example.
